assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant, a judge, posted two messages on his public Facebook page in January 2019 criticizing institutional attacks on key State bodies and endorsing a prosecutor’s public criticism of the justice system (see paragraphs 16-19). In response, the Judicial Inspection Board initiated disciplinary proceedings *ex officio*, and the CSM’s Disciplinary Board for Judges ultimately imposed a two-month 5% pay reduction for impairing the ‘honour and image of the justice system’ under Article 99(a) of Law no. 303/2004 (see paragraphs 20, 24-27). This disciplinary sanction, which targeted the applicant’s extrajudicial expressions of opinion on matters of public interest, clearly constituted an interference with his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 § 1 of the Convention.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference had a basis in domestic law, as it was imposed pursuant to Article 99(a) and Article 100(b) of Law no. 303/2004 on the rules governing judges and public prosecutors (see paragraphs 25-27, 43). This legal framework explicitly defines the disciplinary offence of ‘any behaviour that impairs the honour, the professional integrity or the image of the justice system’ and prescribes proportionate sanctions. The High Court subsequently confirmed that the disciplinary body had correctly applied these provisions in determining the applicant’s liability (see paragraphs 31-33). Consequently, the interference was ‘prescribed by law’ within the meaning of Article 10 § 2 of the Convention.
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The disciplinary sanction pursued the legitimate aim of ‘maintaining the authority and impartiality of the judiciary’, as expressly recognized under Article 10 § 2 of the Convention. The domestic authorities justified the interference on the grounds that the applicant’s Facebook posts — by suggesting political control of State institutions and questioning judicial integrity, while using language deemed improper for a judge — undermined public confidence in the justice system (see paragraphs 27-28, 34-35, 37-38). This aim is consistent with the Convention’s permissible restrictions, as confirmed in the Court’s case-law (see Morissens v. Belgium, no. 11386/05).
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference was not ‘necessary in a democratic society’ and thus failed the proportionality test. First, the applicant’s remarks addressed matters of significant public interest — namely, the perceived politicization of State institutions and threats to constitutional democracy during a period of institutional tension surrounding the Army Chief of Staff’s term extension (see paragraphs 17-18, 23). As a judge and public intellectual, his contributions to such debates are entitled to strong protection under Article 10, particularly where they concern the functioning of the judiciary itself (see CCJE Opinion No. 25 (2022), paragraph 64). Moreover, the High Court acknowledged that his statements did not concern pending cases or identify specific individuals (see paragraph 73), and the dissenting judges on the Disciplinary Board emphasized that forbidding critical commentary on public interest matters would excessively restrict judicial free speech (see paragraph 29). While the applicant’s language in the second post was informal (‘sânge în instalaţie’), it did not incite hatred or Undermine judicial impartiality in a concrete manner. Critically, the domestic authorities relied on the vague and broad concept of ‘impairing the image of the justice system’ (Article 99(a)), which risks a chilling effect on judicial speech (see paragraph 40; cf. Kudeshkina v. Russia, no. 29492/05, where the Court found a violation for similar sanctions based on public criticism of the judiciary). The sanction — though not the most severe — was disproportionate given the lack of a pressing social need to silence such debate, the absence of direct harm to judicial impartiality, and the fact that less restrictive measures (such as a warning) could have sufficed. Therefore, the interference cannot be regarded as necessary in a democratic society (see also Wille v. Liechtenstein [GC], no. 28396/95, § 64, 28 October 1999).
